item.title: NVIDIA Extends DGX Spark Edge AI with TensorRT Edge-LLM and Nemotron-3.5 Lightning
item.description:
NVIDIA Extends DGX Spark Edge AI with TensorRT Edge-LLM and Nemotron-3.5 Lightning

AI workloads are moving beyond the data center. Developers are building agents that run at the edge—monitoring driver attention, helping robots navigate, and coordinating production‑line fleets. These applications must operate within tight memory, power, and latency budgets. NVIDIA now offers the DGX Spark platform in a 64 GB configuration together with the TensorRT Edge‑LLM runtime, enabling developers to prototype, fine‑tune, and test large‑language models such as Nemotron‑3.5 Lightning directly on edge hardware.

🔍 Overview

  • Physical AI agents need compact, low‑latency inference.
  • DGX Spark 64 GB provides the compute and memory headroom for edge prototyping.
  • TensorRT Edge‑LLM delivers a lightweight C++ inference runtime for embedded targets (Jetson Thor, DRIVE AGX Thor, IGX Thor).

🧩 How it works

  • The trtedge command‑line interface (CLI) downloads the selected model (≈21 GB) and builds TensorRT engines optimized for the Spark platform.
  • Once built, engines are cached in ~/.cache/tensorrt-edgellm and reused on later launches.
  • A local OpenAI‑compatible API server can host the model, confirming readiness with a "status":"ready" JSON response.
  • DSpark speculative decoding can be enabled: a draft model proposes several tokens, which the main model validates in a single pass, reducing generation latency.

⚙️ Key details

  • Required software stack: NVIDIA CUDA 13, TensorRT 10.16.1.11 or newer (10.x series), Python 3.10‑3.12.
  • Tested versions: TensorRT Edge‑LLM 0.11.1 and TensorRT 10.16.1.11.
  • Use a Python virtual environment to keep newly installed packages separate while still accessing system‑wide TensorRT libraries.
  • Verify the TensorRT version with the provided check command; if bindings are missing, install the compatible TensorRT 10.x package via the NVIDIA TensorRT pip instructions.
  • First launch downloads the model and builds the engine; subsequent launches reuse cached engines, accelerating startup.

🚀 Performance

  • TensorRT Edge‑LLM with Nemotron‑3.5 Lightning yields low response latency and fast token generation on DGX Spark 64 GB.
  • DSpark speculative decoding (using three draft tokens) improves generation speed; the exact time‑to‑first‑token (TTFT) and token‑per‑second rates are reported in the reference table.
  • Users can tune num_speculative_tokens and other settings to balance speed and accuracy for their workload.

📦 Availability

  • DGX Spark 64 GB configuration is now available for embedded developers.
  • TensorRT Edge‑LLM is released with support for the same inference framework on development (Spark) and deployment platforms such as NVIDIA Jetson Thor, NVIDIA DRIVE AGX Thor, and NVIDIA IGX Thor.
  • The tutorial demonstrates running the text‑only Nemotron‑3.5 Lightning model on Spark and enabling DSpark speculative decoding.

#NVIDIA #EdgeAI #TensorRT #LLM

Source: Run AI Models for Edge Application Development with Just a Few Commands | NVIDIA Technical Blog

item.title: Exowatt Deploys Edge AI Agents for Solar‑Powered Data Center Alarm Triage
item.description:
Exowatt Deploys Edge AI Agents for Solar‑Powered Data Center Alarm Triage

Exowatt has expanded its modular, dispatchable solar platform with AI agents that autonomously triage alarms and perform energy‑market analysis, using a serverless model‑customization pipeline on AWS.

🔍 Overview

  • Exowatt builds modular, dispatchable solar systems for energy‑intensive applications such as AI data centers.
  • The flagship Exowatt P3 captures solar energy with optical lenses, stores it as heat in a long‑duration thermal battery, and dispatches electricity on demand via a heat engine.
  • P3 powers data centers directly behind the meter, avoiding multi‑year grid interconnection queues.
  • A fleet of AI agents monitors live alarms at the edge, where connectivity may be limited or absent.
  • The AI pipeline now turns raw operational data into a certified training set, a fine‑tuned model, and a deployed artifact in days rather than months.

🧩 How it works

Solar system

  • Optical lenses concentrate sunlight onto a thermal absorber.
  • Heat is stored in a thermal battery for long‑duration discharge.
  • A heat engine converts stored heat to electricity on demand.

AI pipeline

  • Raw alarm and market data are collected from each site.
  • Open‑weight base models are fine‑tuned with Low‑Rank Adaptation (LoRA) and supervised fine‑tuning (SFT) on Amazon SageMaker AI.
  • Serverless training allocates capacity on demand, allowing multiple experiments per day.
  • The best model is registered in the SageMaker AI Model Registry and hosted via Amazon Bedrock Custom Model Import.
  • Edge‑deployed models run on no‑GPU controllers; cloud‑deployed models run in the Cloud EMS.

AWS services powering the pipeline

Service Role
Amazon Bedrock Custom Model Import Hosts the fine‑tuned Qwen3‑14B for Cloud EMS (private invocation)
Amazon Bedrock (Qwen3‑VL‑235B) Provides paraphrasing for alarm‑triage
Amazon Bedrock (Claude Sonnet 4.6) Provides paraphrasing for energy‑market analysis
Amazon SageMaker AI (serverless model customization) Fine‑tunes open‑weight base models using LoRA and SFT
Amazon SageMaker AI Model Registry Stores and versions the evaluated deployment artifact

⚙️ Key details

  • Edge alarm‑triage uses the Qwen3‑1.7B model, fine‑tuned for the specific hardware and logic of Exowatt’s EMS.
  • Cloud energy‑market analysis uses the larger Qwen3‑14B model.
  • The fine‑tuned models achieve higher accuracy than frontier models at up to 49× lower cost.
  • Models are small enough to run on edge controllers without GPUs yet accurate enough for autonomous operation.
  • The pipeline can be reused to build smaller, task‑specific models across the growing fleet of sites.

💡 Why it matters

  • Enables data centers to come online quickly without waiting for grid interconnection.
  • Provides reliable alarm monitoring even when connectivity is intermittent.
  • Reduces operational cost by avoiding per‑decision calls to large frontier models.
  • Accelerates model development from months to days, supporting rapid deployment as the fleet scales toward thousands of units.

#Exowatt #AIagents #SolarPower #AWS #EdgeAI

Source: Exowatt beats frontier models on accuracy with SageMaker serverless model customization | Amazon Web Services

item.title: LFM3 Unifies Text, Vision, Audio, Omni, and Decision Models on a 2‑Billion‑Parameter Backbone
item.description:
LFM3 Unifies Text, Vision, Audio, Omni, and Decision Models on a 2‑Billion‑Parameter Backbone

The latest release, LFM3, is the new generation of Liquid Foundation Models that unifies text, vision, audio, omni, and decision capabilities on a shared ~2 B‑parameter backbone.

🔍 Overview

  • LFM3 is built to be the starting point for specialized intelligence.
  • It brings text, vision, audio, omni, and decision models onto one shared backbone, each in the ~2 B‑parameter range.
  • Every modality model branches from LFM3-1.7B-Base.

🧩 How it works

  • Tri‑hybrid architecture: 13 gated short convolutions (kernel size 7), 5 sliding‑window attention layers with a 256‑token window, and 6 global attention layers.
  • Head‑wise gated attention: a sigmoid gate scales each head’s output, allowing a head to switch off when it adds nothing.
  • Partial RoPE: global attention layers rotate only the highest‑frequency half of each head, keeping the other half invariant to distance.
  • Hardware‑in‑the‑loop architecture search redesigns the model for agentic use cases and now covers 14 device and backend combinations, from phones and a Raspberry Pi 5 to laptops, cloud CPUs/GPUs, and the Qualcomm Hexagon NPU.

⚙️ Key Details

  • Parameter efficiency: LFM3‑1.7B outperforms LFM2.5‑2.6B while using 35 % fewer parameters.
  • Speed: With an 8 K‑token context it is about 25 % faster per parameter than LFM2‑1.2B on edge devices.
  • Context window: The text model supports a 256 K‑token window; the final 3.5 T pre‑training tokens extend this window.
  • Pre‑training: 22 T tokens using the same 128 K vocabulary as LFM2.5‑8B‑A1B, with the last 3.5 T tokens emphasizing agentic traces and tool calls.
  • Edge readiness:
    • Text model fits in ~1 GB at 4‑bit precision.
    • Vision encoder combines convolution and attention, using 3× less compute than the SigLIP2 encoder in previous LFM VL models.
    • The 164 M‑parameter vision encoder matches Qwen3.5‑2B’s vision accuracy while requiring 2.2× fewer FLOPs.
    • LiquidCodec audio tokenizer turns generated tokens into speech at ~87× real‑time on a single CPU thread on Apple M4 Max and supports streaming decoding.
  • Fine‑tuning: Any modality model can be fine‑tuned on a single GPU and deployed where the application runs.

Model variants (all derived from LFM3‑1.7B‑Base)

Variant Modality Notable features
Text Text ~1 GB at 4‑bit, 256 K context window, suitable for on‑device agents
Vision Vision Convolution + attention, 3× less compute than SigLIP2, matches Qwen3.5‑2B accuracy with 2.2× fewer FLOPs
Audio Audio Uses LiquidCodec tokenizer, ~87× real‑time speech generation on Apple M4 Max, streaming decoding
Omni Omni First omni model sharing the same backbone
Decision Decision Shares backbone, optimized for agentic tasks

🚀 Availability

  • Models can be fine‑tuned on a single GPU and deployed on the target hardware, including phones, Raspberry Pi 5, laptops, cloud CPUs/GPUs, and the Qualcomm Hexagon NPU.
  • Recommended for local agents, tool calling, structured outputs, or as a base for domain‑specific fine‑tuning.

💡 Why it matters

  • The shared backbone provides more capability per parameter, allowing a 1.7 B‑parameter model to outperform larger predecessors.
  • Unified architecture across modalities reduces the need for separate model families.
  • Edge‑centric design—small size, fast inference, long context—enables advanced agentic tasks to run locally without cloud dependence.

#LiquidFoundationModels #MultimodalAI #EdgeAI #ModelOptimization

Source: Build specialized multimodal models with LFM3

item.title: Updating MLOps Pipelines for Automated Edge Visual Inspection with SageMaker
item.description:
Updating MLOps Pipelines for Automated Edge Visual Inspection with SageMaker

An updated architecture pattern automates fleet-wide computer vision lifecycle management for visual quality inspection at the edge using the Amazon SageMaker Python SDK v3. The solution automates per-camera training, evaluation, compilation, and registration without requiring manual intervention, replacing the deprecated Amazon SageMaker Edge Manager with Amazon SageMaker Neo for edge optimization.

🔍 Overview

When scaling visual inspection from a single proof-of-concept camera to dozens of plant lines with multiple cameras, a single computer vision model trained on pooled footage underperforms. Differences in camera angles, ambient light from bay doors, and glare off stainless surfaces require fine-tuned models for individual cameras. Managing thousands of models manually is impractical, creating the need for automated fleet-wide model lifecycle management.

This update builds on the pattern from the 2023 series Build an end-to-end MLOps pipeline for visual quality inspection at the edge by updating to Amazon SageMaker Python SDK v3 and integrating SageMaker Neo for edge model compilation.

🧩 How it works

Re-training requests arrive via an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) FIFO queue. An AWS Lambda function initiates an AWS Step Functions execution per request, which acquires a slot via a DynamoDB semaphore to limit concurrent executions to at most five by default. This queuing mechanism drains request bursts steadily while keeping concurrent SageMaker training jobs within standard account quotas without needing a quota increase.

Each execution runs a 13-step, dual-branch SageMaker Pipeline parameterized by camera ID:

  • Parallel Entry Steps: Three entry steps execute in parallel: Preprocess, Fetch Latest Anomaly, and Fetch Latest Classifier. Warm-start steps filter by camera ID metadata to resume training from that camera’s specific history.
  • Dual-Branch Training: One branch trains a small convolutional autoencoder that learns normal product appearance and flags anomalies using reconstruction error. The second branch fine-tunes a ResNet18 classifier to confirm defects.
  • Evaluation and Quality Gates: Both branches export trained models to ONNX and evaluate them against held-out data. Quality gates block underperforming models from proceeding.
  • Compilation and Registration: Models passing the quality gate are compiled with SageMaker Neo for the specific edge target and registered in the SageMaker Model Registry as device-ready artifacts.
  • Notifications: Pipeline completions publish to an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic. Operational failures are routed to the same topic via Amazon EventBridge, preserving the original error details.

⚙️ Key details

Pipeline Component Function
Amazon SQS FIFO Queue Queues re-training requests
AWS Lambda & Step Functions Orchestrates pipeline execution flow
DynamoDB Semaphore Restricts concurrency to 5 active jobs to fit standard quotas
Convolutional Autoencoder Learns normal product traits and detects anomalies via reconstruction error
ResNet18 Classifier Fine-tuned model that confirms defects
Amazon SageMaker Neo Compiles ONNX artifacts for specified edge device targets
SageMaker Model Registry Stores versioned, device-optimized model packages
Amazon SNS & EventBridge Handles success notifications and operational failure alerts

💡 Cost and deployment

The entire solution is deployed using the AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK). Note that older CLI versions fail due to a cloud assembly schema mismatch with recent aws-cdk-lib versions. Running a full pipeline execution on synthetic data costs approximately $0.07 in compute, and the complete sample code is published in the aws-samples GitHub repository.

#AWS #SageMaker #MLOps #ComputerVision #EdgeComputing

Source: Fleet-wide computer vision lifecycle at the edge with SageMaker SDK v3 | Amazon Web Services

item.title: LFM2.5-24B-A2B: A Fast On-Device MoE Reasoning Model for Agentic Tasks
item.description:
LFM2.5-24B-A2B: A Fast On-Device MoE Reasoning Model for Agentic Tasks

LFM2.5-24B-A2B is a new reasoning-only model designed for fast, private agentic workflows on-device. Building upon the LFM2-24B-A2B architecture, this update introduces scaled training, expanded context windows, and explicit chain-of-thought reasoning to provide competitive performance against significantly larger models.

🔍 Overview

LFM2.5-24B-A2B is a Mixture of Experts (MoE) model that always produces an explicit chain of thought before providing a final answer. While it is the smallest model in its evaluation group, it is competitive with models like Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, which has ~50% more total and active parameters. Its primary strengths are tool use and instruction following.

🧩 How it works

The model retains its predecessor’s architecture while scaling training and context capabilities:

  • Architecture: 40 layers with 64 experts per MoE block and top-4 routing.
  • Hybrid Design: Uses a combination of gated short convolutions and Grouped Query Attention (GQA).
  • Training Scale: Pre-training was scaled from ~17T to ~33T tokens. Mid-training added 2.3T tokens across 32K and 131K context lengths, emphasizing reasoning, math, and long-context data.
  • Tokenizer: An in-place expansion doubled the vocabulary from 65K to 128K tokens for improved non-Latin tokenization.

⚙️ Key details

Feature Specification
Total Parameters 24 Billion
Active Parameters 2 Billion per token
Context Window 131,000 tokens
Vocabulary Size 128,000 tokens

In benchmark testing, the model leads or matches competition on five of eight tool-use and agentic benchmarks. On LiveClaw, it scored 48.09 compared to 38.19 for Qwen3.6-35B-A3B. On AutomationBench, it scored more than three times the next-best model.

🚀 Availability

LFM2.5-24B-A2B includes day-one support for several inference ecosystems:

  • llama.cpp
  • MLX
  • vLLM
  • SGLang
  • ONNX

💡 Why it matters

This model is optimized for high-speed edge and GPU inference. It decodes at 184 tokens/s on an Apple M5 Max and 114 tokens/s on a Ryzen AI Max+ 395, making it up to 1.7x faster than the next-best compared model while using the least memory. On a single NVIDIA B300 GPU, it can reach over 21,000 output tokens per second. For knowledge-heavy workloads, users are encouraged to pair the model with retrieval or web search, as larger models maintain an edge on benchmarks like GPQA Diamond and SWE-Bench.

#AIagents #EdgeAI #MoE #LiquidFoundationModel

Source: Run fast, private agents on-device with LFM2.5-24B-A2B

item.title: EmbeddingGemma 2 Brings Unified Multimodal Embeddings to On‑Device AI
item.description:
EmbeddingGemma 2 Brings Unified Multimodal Embeddings to On‑Device AI

🔍 Overview

  • Today we are launching EmbeddingGemma 2, a unified multimodal embedding model that expands beyond text to include code, images, video, and audio.
  • Built on the Gemma 4 architecture and released under the Apache 2.0 license, the model has 740 million parameters and is optimized for on‑device inference.

🧩 How it works

  • EmbeddingGemma 2 shares the same text tokenizer and audio encoder as Gemma 4, allowing the two models to run together in a single pipeline with a lower combined memory footprint.
  • The model uses Matryoshka Representation Learning (MRL) so output vectors can be truncated from 768 dimensions down to 512, 256, or 128 dimensions, giving up to 6× storage reduction for local vector databases.

⚙️ Key details

  • Multimodal capabilities – a single model can locate a specific video clip from a voice memo or search hours of audio recordings with a text query.
  • Benchmark performance – achieves leading scores among sub‑1B multimodal embedders on benchmarks such as MTEB Code and MAEB, and matches or outperforms many larger models on text, vision, and audio tasks.
  • Code improvement – code performance jumps 9.92 points on MTEB Code (68.76 → 78.68), making it suitable for local codebase indexing and semantic code search.
  • Modular size options
    Variant Parameters
    Text‑only 270 M
    Vision encoder (optional) 170 M
    Audio encoder (optional) 300 M
  • Extended context – 8 K token window (4× larger than EmbeddingGemma 1), enabling processing of up to 5.5 minutes of audio, 29 images, 58 video frames, or interleaved combinations on local hardware.
  • On‑device efficiency – with quantization, a Google Pixel 11 Pro uses ~191 MB active RAM for text‑only weights and ~567 MB for the full multimodal model.
  • Quality‑per‑parameter – sets a new standard for sub‑1B models across image, video, document, and audio tasks, even outperforming specialist models more than twice its size.

🚀 Availability

  • Model weights are available on Hugging Face and Kaggle; Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform Model Garden will add the model soon.
  • Optimized versions can be found in the LiteRT Community on Hugging Face.
  • Deploy on edge hardware with Google AI Edge MediaPipe (turnkey embedding, retrieval & decision) or LiteRT for custom integration.
  • Build for browsers using transformers.js or WebGPU.
  • Supported runtimes include transformers, sentence‑transformers, MLX, vLLM, llama.cpp, SGLang, Ollama, LMStudio.
  • Store embedding vectors with Qdrant.
  • Fine‑tuning guidance is provided by Unsloth.

💡 Why it matters

  • Generating embeddings locally guarantees data privacy and reduces pipeline latency.
  • Enables fully offline, cross‑modal search and retrieval, empowering developers to build on‑device RAG pipelines that understand complex multimodal data when paired with generative models such as Gemma 4.
  • The developer community’s response to the original EmbeddingGemma exceeded expectations, with more than 20 million downloads used for smarter on‑device search tools and privacy‑first RAG pipelines.

#EmbeddingGemma #MultimodalAI #EdgeAI

Source: EmbeddingGemma 2: an open, lightweight multimodal embedding model

item.title: Offline Voice-First AI Stack Benchmarked on Jetson Orin and Raspberry Pi5
item.description:
Offline Voice-First AI Stack Benchmarked on Jetson Orin and Raspberry Pi5

A new workstream titled Offline AI Modules: Voice-First Offline Architecture, Hardware Reference Stack, Quantization and Benchmarking was submitted on 4 Oct 2026. It delivers a practical, low‑power, community‑accessible solution for voice‑first AI systems that run fully offline.

🔍 Overview

  • Targets African language communities where speech is the dominant interaction mode and internet connectivity is unreliable or absent.
  • Provides three reinforcing components:
    • A modular voice‑first offline architecture.
    • A low‑cost hardware reference bill of materials.
    • A reproducible quantization and benchmarking pipeline for instruction‑tuned language models in the 2‑5 B parameter class.

🧩 How it works

  • The stack is evaluated end‑to‑end across two hardware tiers:
    • Tier B: NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX.
    • Tier A: Raspberry Pi 5.
  • Three instruction‑tuned models are run through four quantization formats.
  • Evaluation metrics include decode throughput, chat latency, memory usage, power consumption, multilingual topic‑classification accuracy (MasakhaNEWS in English, Hausa, Igbo, Nigerian Pidgin, Yoruba), per‑language perplexity drift, and speech‑recognition performance (Ethio‑ASR on Amharic and Oromo).

⚙️ Key details

  • Best trade‑off: Q4_K_M quantization.
  • Performance on Tier B (Jetson Orin NX):
    • Model gemma‑4‑E2B‑it achieves 28.8 t/s decode throughput and 89.2 % topic classification accuracy at Q4_K_M.
  • Performance on Tier A (Raspberry Pi 5):
    • All three models run within a 16 GB memory budget.
Tier Hardware Decode Throughput (t/s) Topic Classification Accuracy Memory Budget
B NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX 28.8 (gemma‑4‑E2B‑it, Q4_K_M) 89.2 % (Q4_K_M) —
A Raspberry Pi 5 — — 16 GB (all models)

🚀 Availability

  • The full paper and benchmark results are available as of the 4 Oct 2026 submission.

💡 Why it matters

  • Enables offline, low‑power voice AI for regions with limited connectivity.
  • Supports a range of African languages, expanding access to speech‑driven technology.
  • Provides a reproducible pipeline that can be adopted by the broader community for similar deployments.

#OfflineAI #VoiceFirst #EdgeAI #AfricanLanguages

Source: Offline AI Modules: Voice-First Offline Architecture, Hardware Reference Stack, Quantization and Benchmarking Source: EMODE: Dynamic Para-Semantic Experts for Emotion-Aware Speech Language Modeling Source: AccentCL: Robust Accent Classification with Incremental Expansion Source: Quality-Aware Self-Correcting Speech Translation on an Edge Device

item.title: 2025 Marks Shift to Autonomous Multi‑Agent AI Systems
item.description:
2025 Marks Shift to Autonomous Multi‑Agent AI Systems

In 2025 the AI landscape moved from passive prompt‑response models to autonomous agents that can plan, code, and validate work without constant human direction.

🔍 Overview

  • Earlier language models waited for explicit human instruction at every computational step.
  • Modern autonomous AI trends establish continuous‑operation paradigms where systems evaluate high‑level objectives, generate internal sub‑goals, and execute complex workflows without constant human oversight.
  • The human role changes from typist to director.

🧩 How it works

  • Agent architecture maintains state and uses scratchpads for intermediate reasoning, looping until validation criteria pass.
  • Probabilistic reasoning engines evaluate environment states, select optimal tools, and modify execution paths dynamically.
  • When data is missing or errors occur, the system queries internal memory, tests alternative APIs, or restructures the execution tree autonomously.
  • Multi‑agent collaboration divides massive operational workloads into manageable micro‑tasks.
Agent Type Role
Planner Evaluates high‑level objectives and creates internal sub‑goals
Coder Generates code to implement the sub‑goals
QA Reviewer Validates output against criteria and provides feedback
  • Frameworks such as LangGraph and AutoGen orchestrate communication protocols between instances.

⚙️ Key details

  • Traditional software runs deterministic branching logic; autonomous systems use probabilistic reasoning and dynamic tool selection.
  • Heavy models run in centralized cloud data centers incur high latency and compute cost.
  • Hardware manufacturers now ship specialized NPUs to consumer and enterprise edge devices, enabling local inference, cutting round‑trip time, and keeping proprietary data off third‑party servers.
  • Autonomous deployment agents monitor CI/CD pipelines, detect performance regressions, isolate faulty micro‑services, patch Kubernetes configurations, and execute zero‑downtime rollouts. Human engineers intervene only for high‑risk architectural changes or policy approvals.
  • Autonomous agents can ingest real‑time shipping telemetry, customs databases, and weather feeds to recalculate optimal routes, renegotiate carrier contracts, and reroute cargo instantly.
  • In finance, agents execute portfolio‑hedging strategies instantly, bypassing human reaction latency during flash crashes or sudden market shifts.

🔒 Security considerations

  • CRITICAL SECURITY WARNING: Autonomous agents with write permissions to production databases or cloud infrastructure are a severe vector for catastrophic failure.
  • Always implement deterministic validation gates and human‑in‑the‑loop checkpoints before executing irreversible write operations, database migrations, or financial transactions that exceed defined thresholds.
  • Restrict agent permissions to scoped, ephemeral tokens with minimal necessary privileges.

💡 Why it matters

  • Shifts AI from reactive text generation to proactive task execution, closing the feedback loop between failure and remediation.
  • Reduces latency, compute cost, and reliance on centralized cloud resources.
  • Enables real‑time adaptation to volatile global trade conditions and fast‑moving financial markets.
  • Allows engineers to focus on strategic decisions rather than routine scripting and debugging.

#AutonomousAI #MultiAgent #EdgeComputing #AIOps

Source: Autonomous AI Trends 2025: Top Tech Drives Next AI Era

item.title: Streamlined Edge ML Workflow for WeBe Band Wearable Device
item.description:
Streamlined Edge ML Workflow for WeBe Band Wearable Device

Researchers have developed a streamlined edge ML workflow to enable the rapid development, optimization, and deployment of machine-learning models directly on the WeBe Band, a wrist-worn device for multimodal physiological data monitoring.

🧩 How it works

The system focuses on system-level automation and deployability, integrating the open-source Piccolo AI ecosystem with an automated pipeline. This framework provides the following capabilities:

  • Hardware-aware model compilation
  • Generation of deployable firmware artifacts
  • Support for over-the-air (OTA) deployment
  • Hardware-aware quantization and AutoML
  • Performance profiling to meet latency targets within device memory and power limitations

⚙️ Key details

The workflow supports multiple lightweight model classes and provides on-device profiling tools to evaluate memory footprint and inference latency under realistic conditions.

Model Class Performance Observations
Classical machine-learning algorithms Offer strong real-time performance
Neural networks Require careful resource management

💡 Why it matters

This work enables researchers and developers to rapidly iterate on models and evaluate them directly on target hardware. While demonstrated on the WeBe Band platform, the workflow is designed to be extensible to other ML-powered edge devices.

#EdgeML #Wearables #AutoML #EmbeddedSystems

Source: A Rapid Pipeline for Training and Deploying ML Models on WeBe Band

item.title: Offloading Physical AI Inference to Edge and Cloud GPUs Improves Robot Performance
item.description:
Offloading Physical AI Inference to Edge and Cloud GPUs Improves Robot Performance

Research indicates that offloading physical AI inference from onboard GPUs to edge or cloud infrastructure can enhance robot performance, battery life, and scalability compared to the prevailing approach of wiring GPUs directly to robots.

💡 Why it matters

Running AI inference exclusively on onboard GPUs introduces several limitations:

  • Power and Weight: GPUs consume significant power, add cost and weight, and can reduce battery life.
  • Hardware Constraints: Some smaller GPUs cannot accommodate the mobile manipulation stack, and onboard GPUs can limit the ability to run the latest generation of AI models.
  • Performance Drops: On GPUs with sufficient memory, mapping and planning slowed by up to 383% compared to an A100. Lighter GPUs caused a 30% drop in timely obstacle detection for navigation and a 50% drop in accuracy for VLA models.
  • Battery Drain: Larger onboard GPUs, such as Jetson Thor, drained robot batteries by up to 160% (or a few hours) for larger robots.

⚙️ Key details

The research focused on mobile robotic manipulation, using canonical tasks such as checking for rubbish in a kitchen and putting it in the trash. The evaluation covered three core capabilities:

Capability Impact of Offloading
Semantic mapping and planning Improved response time and accuracy; reduced slowdowns compared to onboard GPUs
Navigation Improved timely detection of obstacles
Manipulation Improved task success rates and accuracy

Replacing power-hungry onboard compute with lightweight hardware, such as a Raspberry Pi-5 board, and shipping data to an offloaded GPU substantially improves battery lifetime.

🧩 How it works

A new toolset has been developed to facilitate the distribution of inference between the robot, edge GPUs, and the cloud:

  • Orchestration: Uses Kubernetes-based tooling to provide a uniform abstraction for distributing robotic AI workloads.
  • Deployment: Allows for automatic containerization and offloading using declarative specifications and smart policies.
  • Integration: The toolset integrates with ROS2, LeRobot, and robotic simulators for development.

#PhysicalAI #Robotics #EdgeComputing #Kubernetes #DistributedInference

Source: What if robots didn’t need all their AI onboard?

item.title: NVIDIA TensorRT Edge-LLM Performance in MLPerf Inference v6.1 Edge Agentic Benchmark
item.description:
NVIDIA TensorRT Edge-LLM Performance in MLPerf Inference v6.1 Edge Agentic Benchmark

NVIDIA TensorRT Edge-LLM has completed the MLPerf Inference v6.1 Edge Agentic benchmark running the Qwen3.6-27B model on a single NVIDIA Jetson AGX Thor Developer Kit.

⚙️ Key details

The system was configured with the following specifications:

  • Hardware: One NVIDIA Jetson AGX Thor Developer Kit
  • Memory: 128 GB of unified memory
  • Power Mode: MAXN
  • Execution Mode: SingleStream
  • Model: Qwen3.6-27B

📊 Performance results

The TensorRT Edge-LLM submission completed the performance workload in 24 minutes and 36 seconds, which is 6.4x faster than the llama.cpp reference submission of 2 hours and 37 minutes.

Metric Value
Output throughput 52.33 tokens per second
Median time to first token 247.12 ms
Median time per output token 14.68 ms
BFCL overall accuracy 87.94%

🧩 How it works

The result was achieved using several optimization techniques:

  • Quantization: The submission used NVFP4 (a 4-bit floating-point format supported by the NVIDIA Blackwell GPU) for weights and activations, including the language-model head, and FP8 for the KV cache. This smaller representation increases available unified memory for application workloads, speculative decoding state, and long context.
  • KV Cache Reuse: TensorRT Edge-LLM identifies reusable prompt prefixes and restores cached attention KV pages. Because Qwen3.6 uses a hybrid model architecture, the runtime also restores partial KV-page state and the recurrent state. In this workload, approximately 96% of prompt tokens were served with hot cache, requiring the prefill of only ~0.5M of the 13.6M total prompt tokens.
  • Tree-based Multi-Token Prediction (MTP): A draft model predicts several future tokens which the target model verifies together in one forward pass. The server configuration utilized:
    • 8 draft steps
    • Top-2 candidates at each drafting depth
    • A 16-node verification tree

🔍 Overview

The MLPerf Edge Agentic benchmark measures OpenAI-compatible model endpoints across two phases:

  • Performance: The workload consists of 20 conversations and 1,007 generated turns. Input length grows to approximately 23.5K tokens.
  • Accuracy: This phase uses Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard (BFCL) v4 prompts with reasoning off and single-turn only to balance evaluation time and accuracy on edge devices.

#MLPerf #TensorRT #JetsonAGXThor #EdgeAI #LLM

Source: TensorRT Edge-LLM Completes the MLPerf Edge Agentic Benchmark 6.4x Faster on Jetson AGX Thor | NVIDIA Technical Blog

EMMI Enables Communication-Efficient MLLM Inference for Edge Intelligence

Edge Multi-Modal Intelligence (EMMI) has been developed to enable multimodal large language model (MLLM) reasoning on resource-constrained edge platforms by utilizing fused representation compression.

🔍 Overview

Deploying MLLMs on edge platforms is challenging due to substantial memory, communication, and computational demands. EMMI addresses these constraints by communicating a compact representation between edge devices and server resources rather than transmitting raw sensor observations or partitioning neural networks at intermediate layers.

🧩 How it works

EMMI utilizes a representation-centric design that involves the following steps at the edge:

  • Modality-specific encoding
  • Cross-modal representation fusion
  • Learned compression

Only the resulting compact latent representation is transmitted to server-side resources for high-capacity MLLM reasoning.

💡 Why it matters

The EMMI approach provides several operational advantages:

  • Efficiency: Reduces communication overhead.
  • Privacy: Preserves local data privacy.
  • Interoperability: Provides a fixed-size interface between server-side MLLMs and heterogeneous edge devices.

⚙️ Key details

Evaluation on a representative multimodal benchmark shows the following performance improvements under bandwidth-constrained edge conditions:

Metric Result
Communication payload reduction 32x
Estimated end-to-end inference latency reduction Up to 3.4x
Accuracy Maintains comparable downstream accuracy

#EMMI #MLLM #EdgeIntelligence #MachineLearning

item.title: 🚀 Kernels: The Secret Sauce Making ML Models Faster and 8-16x More Compact
item.description:
🚀 Kernels: The Secret Sauce Making ML Models Faster and 8-16x More Compact

Summary: Explore how the Kernels project slashes AI model sizes by 8-16x while improving inference speed through innovative kernel functions that eliminate computational waste. Learn why this open-source approach to quantization matters for democratizing AI deployment across diverse hardware.

🌟 Revolutionizing Model Efficiency with Kernels

Machine learning models are getting bigger, more powerful, and increasingly resource-hungry. The consequence? Deploying state-of-the-art AI has become a privilege reserved for those with access to industrial-grade hardware and infrastructure. But what if we could dramatically shrink these models while maintaining their capabilities or even making them faster?

Enter Kernels – an innovative open-source project that’s tackling the efficiency challenge head-on.

The 𝗸𝗲𝗿𝗻𝗲𝗹𝘀 project introduces a radical approach to model quantization, reducing model sizes by 8-16x while simultaneously improving inference speed. This breakthrough comes at a critical moment when the AI community is grappling with models that demand ever-increasing computational resources.

🧩 What Makes Kernels Special?

Traditional quantization approaches often face a painful tradeoff between model size and performance. The 𝙠𝙚𝙧𝙣𝙚𝙡𝙨 project takes a fundamentally different approach by reimagining how computations happen at the most fundamental level.

🔍 Kernel Functions: The Core Innovation

The magic lies in specialized kernel functions that eliminate computational redundancy. Here’s how it works:

  1. Targeted Optimization: Rather than applying generic compression techniques across the entire model, 𝗸𝗲𝗿𝗻𝗲𝗹𝘀 identifies and optimizes the most computation-intensive operations.

  2. Precision Without Waste: By carefully analyzing what precision levels are actually needed for different model components, 𝙠𝙚𝙧𝙣𝙚𝙡𝙨 applies just the right amount of precision where it matters most.

  3. Hardware Awareness: The kernel functions are designed with modern hardware architectures in mind, ensuring that the theoretical efficiency gains translate to real-world performance improvements.

🚀 Quantization with a Difference

What truly sets 𝗸𝗲𝗿𝗻𝗲𝗹𝘀 apart is how it approaches quantization:

1
2

Traditional approach: Convert all weights to lower precision uniformly
Kernels approach: Tailor precision levels based on computational impact

This tailored approach means that critical pathways in the model retain necessary precision while less sensitive areas can be dramatically compressed. The result? Models that are a fraction of their original size but maintain comparable or sometimes even improved performance characteristics.

💡 Real-world Impact and Applications

The implications of this technology extend far beyond academic interest – they fundamentally change what’s possible in practical AI deployment:

🏆 Democratizing Advanced AI

With models shrunk by 8-16x, advanced AI becomes accessible to a much wider range of devices and users. Imagine running sophisticated language models on consumer laptops or even smartphones without crushing performance issues.

⚡ Faster Inference, Lower Costs

The efficiency gains translate directly to faster inference times and significantly reduced operational costs. For large-scale deployments, this could mean:

  • Lower cloud computing bills
  • Reduced energy consumption
  • Smaller carbon footprint
  • More responsive user experiences

🌐 Edge Computing Revolution

Perhaps most exciting is how 𝙠𝙚𝙧𝙣𝙚𝙡𝙨 could accelerate the push toward edge computing. By making models compact enough to run locally on devices, we can address critical issues around privacy, latency, and connectivity constraints.

🔮 Looking Forward: The Open Source Advantage

What makes the 𝗸𝗲𝗿𝗻𝗲𝗹𝘀 project particularly promising is its open-source nature. This approach ensures:

  1. Community Improvement: The technology can evolve through contributions from researchers and practitioners worldwide.

  2. Adaptability: The methods can be applied across different model architectures and use cases.

  3. Accessibility: No proprietary barriers limit who can benefit from these advancements.

As AI continues to permeate every aspect of our digital lives, technologies like 𝙠𝙚𝙧𝙣𝙚𝙡𝙨 become increasingly crucial. They represent not just technical optimizations but a path toward more sustainable, accessible, and democratized artificial intelligence.

🤔 Final Thoughts

The 𝗸𝗲𝗿𝗻𝗲𝗹𝘀 project reminds us that innovation in AI isn’t just about creating bigger models with more parameters – it’s also about making our existing capabilities more efficient and accessible.

As we navigate the exciting but challenging frontier of AI development, approaches that prioritize efficiency without sacrificing performance will be essential. The question now becomes: How will you incorporate these quantization techniques into your own machine learning workflows to make your models lighter, faster, and more deployable?

item.title: Beyond Expectations: Running Real-Time Conversational AI Locally with GLTF Avatar Animation
item.description:
🔮 Beyond Expectations: Running Real-Time Conversational AI Locally with GLTF Avatar Animation

Summary: Discover how local conversational AI models are exceeding performance expectations and explore the exciting frontier of integrating these models with 3D avatar animations through ThreeJS and GLTF in browsers.

🚀 The Surprising Power of Local AI Implementations

When it comes to conversational AI, we’ve grown accustomed to cloud-dependent solutions that require constant internet connectivity and raise privacy concerns. But what if I told you that running these sophisticated models 100% locally is not only possible—it’s impressively effective?

“𝘛𝘩𝘪𝘴 𝘸𝘰𝘳𝘬𝘴 𝘸𝘢𝘺 𝘣𝘦𝘵𝘵𝘦𝘳 𝘵𝘩𝘢𝘯 𝘐 𝘦𝘹𝘱𝘦𝘤𝘵𝘦𝘥!” This revelation isn’t just exciting—it’s transformative for how we conceptualize AI integration in everyday applications.

Local AI processing is experiencing a renaissance moment. Modern devices pack enough computational power to handle increasingly optimized models without sacrificing performance. The advantages are compelling:

  • 🔒 Enhanced privacy with data never leaving your device
  • ⚡ Zero latency from network communication
  • 🌐 Offline functionality in any environment
  • 💰 Reduced operational costs without cloud processing fees

The initial success of these local implementations naturally leads to the question: what’s next? The answer appears to be bringing these conversational models to life through visual representation.

🤖 The Next Frontier: Animated AI Avatars

The logical progression from effective local conversational AI is visual embodiment. As noted in the original observation: “𝙎𝙤 𝙩𝙝𝙚𝙣 𝙩𝙝𝙚 𝙣𝙚𝙭𝙩 𝙤𝙗𝙫𝙞𝙤𝙪𝙨 𝙨𝙩𝙚𝙥 𝙞𝙨 𝙖𝙫𝙖𝙩𝙖𝙧 𝙖𝙣𝙞𝙢𝙖𝙩𝙞𝙤𝙣…𝙨𝙤𝙢𝙚𝙝𝙤𝙬.”

This integration introduces fascinating technical challenges and opportunities. For browser-based applications, the technology stack seems clearly defined:

  • 📦 GLTF (GL Transmission Format) avatars as the 3D model standard
  • 🎭 ThreeJS as the rendering engine
  • 🗣️ Phoneme animation to synchronize speech with facial movements

GLTF has emerged as the “JPEG of 3D” for good reason. The format efficiently packages textures, materials, and animations in a web-friendly way, making it ideal for browser-based AI avatars.

🧩 Building the Technical Stack for Animated AI Companions

Let’s explore what this integration might look like from a technical perspective.

The Foundation: Local Conversational AI

At the core is a lightweight, optimized language model capable of running entirely on-device. Recent innovations in model quantization, pruning, and architecture optimization have made this possible even on modest hardware. These models can process natural language, generate contextually appropriate responses, and maintain conversation state without external dependencies.

const conversation = model.createConversation();

function handleUserInput(text) {
 const response = await conversation.getResponse(text);
 generateSpeech(response);
 animateAvatar(response);
}

The Visual Layer: ThreeJS and GLTF

ThreeJS provides the perfect foundation for rendering 3D content in browsers with WebGL. Combined with GLTF models, you can create expressive avatars that run smoothly across devices:

// Pseudocode for setting up a ThreeJS avatar
const scene = new THREE.Scene();
const loader = new GLTFLoader();

loader.load('avatar.gltf', (gltf) => {
 const avatar = gltf.scene;
 scene.add(avatar);

 // Extract animation mixers and facial morphs
 const mixer = new THREE.AnimationMixer(avatar);
 const morphTargetDictionary = avatar.morphTargetDictionary;
});

The Animation Challenge: Phoneme Mapping

The most technically complex piece is synchronizing speech with facial movements through phoneme animation. Phonemes—the distinct units of sound in language—need to be mapped to facial expressions:

 // Convert text to phoneme sequence with timing
 const phonemes = textToPhonemes(text);

 // For each phoneme, animate the corresponding facial morph target
 phonemes.forEach(({phoneme, startTime, duration}) => {
 setTimeout(() => {
 const morphIndex = morphTargetDictionary[phonemeToMorphMap[phoneme]];
 avatar.morphTargetInfluences[morphIndex] = 1.0;

 // Blend to next phoneme
 setTimeout(() => {
 avatar.morphTargetInfluences[morphIndex] = 0.0;
 }, duration);
 }, startTime);
 });
}

🔍 Real-World Applications and Future Potential

This technology combination opens doors to numerous applications:

  • 🎓 Educational assistants with engaging visual presence
  • 🏥 Healthcare companions for patient interaction
  • 🛒 Retail customer service with personalized avatars
  • 🎮 Gaming NPCs with dynamic conversational abilities
  • 🌐 Accessible web interfaces for diverse user needs

The most exciting aspect is how this technology democratizes access to embodied AI. Rather than requiring specialized hardware or expensive cloud services, these solutions can run on common devices already in users’ hands.

🌟 Looking Forward: The Human Touch

As we develop these avatar-enhanced conversational systems, the key challenge will be balancing technical capability with human-like interaction. The uncanny valley—that unsettling feeling when something appears almost but not quite human—remains a significant hurdle.

The path forward likely involves:

  1. 🎨 Stylized rather than photorealistic avatars
  2. 🎭 Expressive but not exaggerated animations
  3. 🧠 Context-aware emotional responses
  4. 🔄 Natural conversation flow with appropriate pauses and reactions

What’s particularly exciting about this development is how it bridges the gap between pure text interaction and fully embodied AI. The combination of local processing power with visual representation creates a more engaging, accessible AI experience.

As these technologies continue to mature, we might soon find ourselves having meaningful conversations with AI companions that not only understand what we’re saying but respond with appropriate facial expressions and gestures—all running entirely on our personal devices.

The question now becomes: how will these visual representations shape our relationships with AI systems? Will animated avatars create stronger emotional connections to artificial intelligence, and how might that transform our digital interactions?
